topic: Sorting shastra from folklore — Lakshmi yoga and the 'Kubera' claims (DD deep-dive reel, English, 2026-09-02 pm)

slides.sub: One of these is in the texts. The other was invented for a thumbnail.

slides.body:
A shastric yoga has three things: a named source, a precise definition you can check against a chart, and stated conditions under which it fails.

Folklore has a name and a promise, and nothing in between. If nobody can tell you which text it comes from or what would cancel it, you are not looking at a technique.

Classical definition: the 9th lord — lord of the house of fortune — placed in a kendra (the angles 1, 4, 7, 10) or a trikona (the trines 1, 5, 9), in its own sign or exaltation, together with a strong lagna lord.

Note how much is load-bearing. Not "9th lord somewhere decent". Own sign or exaltation, angular or trinal, and a strong lagna lord. Drop any clause and it is no longer the yoga.

points: Combustion — a participating planet too close to the Sun loses its say
Debility in Navamsa (D9) — the ninth-part chart, read for underlying strength
Dusthana placement — the yoga sitting in the 6th, 8th or 12th is muffled
No dasha — the planetary period system; without one, the yoga never activates

slides.body:
Kubera is a deity — the lord of wealth in Puranic tradition, entirely real as devotional material. What does not exist is a standard classical yoga of that name with a fixed definition in the Jyotish texts.

The phrase circulates because it sells. Ask for the source and the cancellation clauses, and there are none — which is exactly the test on slide 2, failed.

Devotion to Kubera is one thing and needs no defence. Attaching a deity's name to a chart claim in order to sell a remedy is another.

The classical material is stricter than the internet version, not looser. Every genuine wealth yoga in the texts arrives with conditions attached — folklore drops the conditions and keeps the promise.

No yoga guarantees wealth. Not Lakshmi yoga with every condition satisfied, and certainly not one that was invented last year.

Jyotish describes a tendency and a season, never an outcome. Anyone promising money from a yoga name is skipping the conditions the texts themselves insist on.

Source? Definition? Cancellation clauses? Three questions, and most viral yogas fail all three.

Comment a yoga name you have been sold, and save this reel — slide 2 is the whole filter.
